% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
LLM-generated text increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, and the resulting recursive chains progressively diverge from human-written text.
We ask whether this drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Studying eight base (pretrained) models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): central-tendency features (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drift monotonically with generation depth, while shape features (entropy max, vocabulary tail slope) remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution that approximately preserves distributional shape.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains (five-generator subset), using a single 410M-parameter reference model.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, which restricts current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We introduced generation depth classification and documented a differential depth response across eight base-model generators from five families: recursive generation is consistent with a systematic location shift in the token-level NLL distribution that approximately preserves distributional shape.
5	A lightweight 7-feature ensemble detects this drift with leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator LOGO evaluation (0.764 on cross-model chains; five-generator subset).
6	The signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning and may further compress at larger scales (our largest generator is 8B); these limitations define the current scope boundaries.
7	All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication.
8

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	The near-stationarity of shape features is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
5	Sampling ablation supports this as a tendency rather than a guarantee ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and prompt-type dependence further modulates the effect (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
6	
7	Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints in preliminary experiments (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base, 6-generator LOGO): alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation that DDR exploits.
8	This restricts current applicability to base models and constitutes the primary scope limitation.
9	At the document level within base models, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging; the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary concentrates 86\% of binary errors as false negatives, with larger generators exacerbating this (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
10	Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially ($t{=}0.7 \to t{=}1.0$: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
11	
12	Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling: 5-class F1 drops to ${\approx}$0.50 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), and ordinal-specific methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}). These results suggest that the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary rather than ordinal structure is the bottleneck.
13	DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, is fully reversible, and approximately preserves distributional shape. This pattern suggests compression within existing capacity rather than erosion of it.
14

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The near-stationarity of shape features is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
Sampling ablation supports this as a tendency rather than a guarantee ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and prompt-type dependence further modulates the effect (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).

Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints in preliminary experiments (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base, 6-generator LOGO): alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation that DDR exploits.
This restricts current applicability to base models and constitutes the primary scope limitation.
At the document level within base models, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging; the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary concentrates 86\% of binary errors as false negatives, with larger generators exacerbating this (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially ($t{=}0.7 \to t{=}1.0$: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).

Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling: 5-class F1 drops to ${\approx}$0.50 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), and ordinal-specific methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}). These results suggest that the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary rather than ordinal structure is the bottleneck.
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, is fully reversible, and approximately preserves distributional shape. This pattern suggests compression within existing capacity rather than erosion of it.

This is the **primary scope limitation**.\\n2. **Temperature sensitivity**: Reliable within t ∈ [0.5, 0.9] (≤1 pp degradation from default t=0.7). Acknowledge explicitly.\\n- Do NOT use H1/H2 terminology. ## Target Venue

## Core Insight
Non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains exhibit **differential depth response** (DDR): **central-tendency/diversity features** (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with depth, while **shape features** (entropy_max, tail_decay) remain near-stationary. This is consistent with recursive generation inducing a **location shift** in the NLL distribution while approximately preserving distributional shape. The contribution is: (a) the **task formulation** (generation depth classification beyond binary detection), (b) **empirical validation** across 8 generators / 5 model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B–8B) showing DDR is robust, (c) a lightweight 7-feature ensemble achieving leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO. Depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current scope to base models.

## Core Claims (3 条，均可证伪)

**Claim 1 — Depth Discriminability**: A 7-feature distributional ensemble can classify generation depth (gen-0 / gen-1 / gen-2+) with leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 (95% CI [0.688, 0.700]) under 8-generator LOGO evaluation, generalizing across unseen generators and model families (LOFO binary F1 = 0.686). Cross-model chains yield binary F1 = 0.764. Primary metric is leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs gen-2+), excluding gen-0 to avoid seed-sharing leakage.

**Claim 2 — Differential Depth Response & Feature Complementarity**: Features exhibit DDR: drifting features show |ρ| > 0.60 (hapax −0.63, TTR −0.61, entropy_mean −0.60), while shape features show |ρ| < 0.10 (tail_decay 0.04). KS statistics confirm: drifting 0.516–0.537 vs shape 0.043–0.052 (~10× gap). Full 7-feature set (10-fold CV F1 = 0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar p ≈ 0). Reference-only yields higher binary F1 (0.833 vs 0.695) but surface features are essential for 3-class gen-0 discrimination.

**Claim 3 — Downstream Utility (Negative Finding)**: Depth-aware data curation does NOT improve downstream CLM quality. At equal sample count (n=3,951): random subsampling (ppl=2.367) outperforms depth 0–1 (2.387) and binary-filtered (2.389). TOST confirms equivalence at ±2% margin (p = 1.1×10⁻⁴). Full dataset (n=12,299, ppl=2.335) vs depth-filtered requires ±3% margin for equivalence. Depth fingerprinting is a **diagnostic** tool for provenance characterization, not a **curative** tool for data selection.

## Headline Metrics Summary

| Metric | Value | Context |
|--------|-------|---------|
| **Primary: LOGO binary F1** | **0.694** [0.688, 0.700] | 8-gen LOGO, gen-1 vs gen-2+, leak-free |
| LOGO 3-class F1 | 0.762 [0.758, 0.766] | Inflated by gen-0 seed sharing |
| Cross-model binary F1 | 0.764 | 5-gen subset, 5-fold CV |
| Cross-model 3-class F1 | 0.809 | 5-gen subset, 5-fold CV |
| LOFO binary F1 | 0.686 | Leave-one-family-out |
| Per-gen binary F1 range | 0.633–0.724 | Mistral-7B lowest, Pythia-2.8B highest |
| Feature ablation (10-fold CV) | Full 0.773, Surface 0.688, Ref 0.713 | McNemar p ≈ 0 |
| Length-matched binary F1 | 0.724 vs 0.770 unmatched | Deconfounding, not sample-size effect |

## Scope & Limitations (必须在论文中突出)

1. **Base models only**: Instruct-tuned models show substantially degraded signal (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1 = 0.338 vs 0.763 base). Alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation DDR exploits. This is the **primary scope limitation**.
2. **Temperature sensitivity**: Reliable within t ∈ [0.5, 0.9] (≤1 pp degradation from default t=0.7). At t = 1.0: −6 pp degradation; entropy_mean ρ drops from −0.60 to −0.002. Cross-temperature transfer degrades severely (t=0.7 → t=1.0: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops 0.789 → 0.418).
3. **7-feature ensemble is not optimal**: Multi-detector ensembles (4-det + surface) achieve 3-class 0.795 vs 0.774 (+2.1 pp) and binary 0.708 vs 0.705 (+0.3 pp), but at 2.4× inference cost and 3.2× GPU memory. 7-feature positioned on **efficiency advantage**, not absolute performance.
4. **3-class resolution ceiling**: 5-class F1 drops to ~0.50; ordinal methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost. Gen-1/gen-2+ boundary is the bottleneck (concentrates 86% of binary errors as FNs).
5. **Scale effect**: Larger generators show moderate degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633, Qwen3-8B: 0.692 vs average 0.694). Higher-capacity models compress feature margins.
6. **Prompt-type dependence**: Continuation chains show stronger drift (F1 = 0.781) than elaboration (0.730).

## Story Spine

**Problem**: Web-scraped training data increasingly contains LLM-generated text of unknown provenance depth (7–17% of recent scientific papers). Current detection methods offer only binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material: gen-1 retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score) cannot distinguish gen-1 from gen-2+. Attractor cycle theory (ACL 2025) bounds paraphrasing chains to ~3 classes but depends on semantic-preservation constraints. No existing method addresses generation depth estimation in non-paraphrastic continuation chains. When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, single detector scores show moderate signal but high cross-generator variance.

**Our framing**: We formulate generation depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) and characterize DDR across 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B). Central-tendency features drift monotonically while shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution. A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under 8-gen LOGO with a single 410M reference model. Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 at 2.4× cost. The signal degrades under instruction tuning and high temperature, restricting current scope to base models at moderate temperatures.

**Headline result template**: "On 8 base-model generators from 5 families (0.6B–8B), our 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under LOGO evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M reference model. **RC1 — "Is this just vocabulary impoverishment?"**: Surface features alone achieve 0.688, but full features achieve 0.773 (McNemar p ≈ 0). Reference features capture different, complementary signal. **RC5 — "What about human editing?"**: Robustness test with simulated human edits (random word replacement + LLM-simulated editing). Reported in appendix.

**RC6 — "Ecological validity?"**: Multi-domain seeds (news, Wikipedia, scientific, creative) + multiple prompt types (continuation, elaboration, rewriting). Prompt-type dependence reported transparently (continuation 0.781 vs elaboration 0.730).

**RC8 — "Aren't these just OOD detection features?"**: Contribution is NOT the features but: (a) ordinal depth estimation formulation, (b) empirical DDR discovery (drifting vs stationary), (c) Findings-level empirical characterization. **RC9 — "Only base models — what about instruct?"**: Acknowledged as primary limitation. OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1 = 0.338 vs 0.763 base. Instruction tuning compresses the distributional variation DDR exploits. Reported transparently; defines scope boundary.

The contribution is **empirical and conceptual**, appropriate for Findings:
1. **Problem formulation**: Generation depth classification as a new task beyond binary detection (no prior work addresses this in non-paraphrastic chains)
2. **Empirical characterization**: DDR across 8 generators / 5 families (0.6B–8B), with cross-generator generalization (LOGO binary F1 = 0.694, LOFO 0.686, cross-model 0.764). Honest reporting of scope boundaries (instruct degradation, temperature sensitivity, scale effect).
3. **Negative finding**: Depth-aware curation ≡ random subsampling for downstream quality (TOST confirmed). Depth fingerprinting is diagnostic, not curative.

- Do NOT call the drift/stationarity split a "discovery" — it follows from location-shift properties of the NLL distribution. Acknowledge explicitly.
- Do NOT use H1/H2 terminology. Use "drifting" vs "stationary" or "differential response."
- Do NOT overclaim "dual dynamics." Use "differential depth response" (DDR).
- Report **realistic performance range** (binary F1 0.633–0.724 per-generator, 0.694 LOGO average) in abstract/conclusion, not best-case.
- Primary metric is leak-free binary F1 (not 3-class, which is inflated by gen-0 seed sharing).
- 7-feature ensemble is positioned on efficiency, not absolute superiority over multi-detector ensembles.

Related work must cover: perplexity-based detection (DetectGPT, GLTR, DNA-GPT, Binoculars), model collapse theory, OOD detection, data quality scoring, watermarking, vocabulary diversity, stylometry/authorship attribution, iterative generation (LLM as Broken Telephone ACL 2025), membership inference.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), which suggests that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), which indicates that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

Depth Fingerprinting: Detecting Recursive Generation Depth in Base LLM Text Chains

## Abstract

LLM-generated text increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, and the resulting recursive chains progressively diverge from human-written text. We ask whether this drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as generation depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic). Studying eight base (pretrained) models from five families (0.6B-8B parameters), we identify a differential depth response (DDR): central-tendency features (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drift monotonically with generation depth, while shape features (entropy max, vocabulary tail slope) remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution that approximately preserves distributional shape. A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains (five-generator subset), using a single 410M-parameter reference model. The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, which restricts current applicability to base models.

Word count: ~146

## Keywords

generation depth classification, LLM text detection, recursive generation chains, differential depth response, distributional fingerprinting, text provenance, cross-generator generalization

## AI Assistance Disclosure Statement

We used AI writing assistants (Claude, GPT-4) for language polishing, code debugging, and LaTeX formatting during the preparation of this manuscript. All scientific contributions, including the problem formulation, experimental design, data analysis, and conclusions, are the authors' own work. AI tools were not used to generate experimental results or data.

## Responsible NLP Research Checklist

### A. Limitations

**A1. Did you discuss the limitations of your work?**
Yes. A dedicated Limitations section (unnumbered, after the Conclusion) discusses: (1) restriction to base models with instruct-tuned degradation quantified (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1 = 0.338 vs. 0.763 base); (2) temperature sensitivity (reliable at t in [0.5, 0.9], substantial degradation at t = 1.0); (3) scale ceiling (largest generator 8.2B, frontier models untested); (4) prompt-type dependence (continuation F1 = 0.781 vs. elaboration 0.730); (5) 3-class resolution limit (5-class F1 drops to ~0.50); (6) English-only evaluation; (7) reference model dependency.

### B. Potential Risks

**B1. Did you discuss potential risks of your work?**
Yes. The Ethics Statement discusses that the method estimates generation depth, not author identity, with minimal privacy implications. We acknowledge the risk that depth estimation tools could be used to suppress legitimate machine-generated content and encourage deployment for provenance transparency rather than content removal.

### C. Compute Resources

**C1. Did you report the computational budget?**
Yes. Ethics Statement reports: 4x NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs (32 GB each), approximately 62 GPU-hours total. Software versions are fully specified (Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.10.0/CUDA 12.8, Transformers 4.57.6, XGBoost 3.2.0, scikit-learn 1.8.0).

### D. Human Subjects

**D1. Did the research involve human subjects?**
No. All texts are LLM-generated from publicly available Wikipedia seeds. No human annotation, crowdsourcing, or human evaluation was conducted.

### E. Dataset and Licensing

**E1. Did you report dataset licenses?**
Yes. Ethics Statement reports: Wikipedia seed passages under CC BY-SA 3.0. All generator models under permissive licenses (Apache 2.0 for Pythia, OLMo, Mistral; Qwen License for Qwen3; Llama Community License for Llama 3.2).

**E2. Did you provide dataset statistics?**
Yes. Appendix A provides full dataset statistics including sample counts per generator, depth, and prompt type.

### F. Code and Reproducibility

**F1. Will you release code and data?**
Yes. All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication.

**F2. Did you provide sufficient detail to reproduce your results?**
Yes. The Method section specifies all feature definitions, classifier hyperparameters, evaluation protocols (LOGO, LOFO, cross-model), and decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus p = 0.9). Appendices provide ablations for sampling sensitivity, classifier choice, and feature selection.

### G. Existing Artifacts

**G1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you use?**
Yes. All generator models (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen3, Llama 3.2, Mistral), evaluation tools, and relevant prior work are cited.
